As someone rightly observed, complete knowledge of even the smallest blade of grass would necessarily give us complete knowledge of the structure of the universe as a whole.
But people usually forgot something here.
The real universe contains not only every real and material thing but also every person who actually lives within it, together with their consciousness, knowledge, thoughts, speech, and so on.
If my desk outside my room is an abstraction, then a desk without my body sitting beside it is just as much an abstraction.
And this body contains my I, which not only allows the body to put its weight on the desk but also allows it to write definite and meaningful words on it.
All of this plainly forms part of the concrete reality of my desk—and of the universe.
More generally, since the only things we know are things we actually know, the thing we know is not simply a material “thing.” It is also a thing known by me.
A “thing without my knowledge of it” is an abstraction in exactly the same sense as a “thing outside the universe.”
We should emphasize once again, however, that this is true only when we are dealing either with a concrete thing—that is, a real or material thing—or with a concrete human being.

When we are dealing with an ideal “thing,” meaning something abstract and non-material, it is perfectly possible to know everything that can be known about it without knowing anything definite about other things, whether ideal or real.

We can see this simply by remembering that it is possible, for example, to know all the geometrical properties of a triangle without knowing algebra, Russian, the structure of the atom, or the structure of the universe.

The same is true of the properties of the “table in general.” We can know the word, concept, or idea of “table” without knowing anything about particular people, particular tables, the universe, and so on.
Only complete and concrete knowledge of concrete things or human beings therefore necessarily becomes universal or perfect knowledge.
The example of my desk has shown that this is true of concrete things. We can now see, by taking myself as the example, that it is equally true of concrete human beings.
If I want to give an exhaustive answer to the concrete question “Who am I?”, then among other things I must say that I am this person who is, at this moment, sitting at his desk and writing.
So my knowledge of myself must include knowledge of the table—and therefore, as we have just seen, knowledge of the material universe as a whole, including my body.
But I must also speak about my I and its contents.
Those contents are my thoughts—that is, meaningful words or concepts, ideas.
And it is easy to see that complete knowledge of the contents that make up my I includes knowledge of the entire ideal world.
For what I do not know—mathematics or Greek, for example—characterizes me just as much as what I do know.
And to know what I do not know, one would have to know the whole ideal world.
Complete, concrete knowledge of one concrete human being therefore includes complete knowledge of both the real world and the ideal world.
It also includes complete knowledge of that person’s human I, which forms the point of connection between those two worlds.
It is easy to see that such knowledge is nothing other than complete knowledge of the entire human or historical world from the “beginning of time” down to the present moment.
My I is characterized, among other things, by the fact that I am writing now—that is, that I am translating concepts from ideal existence into real existence, turning them into marks on paper.
And I am writing precisely what I am, in fact, writing.
But I could not write what I am writing if I had not read Hegel.
Hegel, in turn, could not have written what he wrote if he had not read Kant, and so on.
And the “first” philosopher could not have philosophized unless he had already been able to speak.
So once again we have to trace the path back from the “first” philosopher to the “first” human being who began to speak.

That human being appeared on Earth when, “for the first time,” certain animals began to speak—why they did so we will learn later. In other words, we have to go all the way back to the “first” human being as such.
To know completely what my concrete human I is, I therefore have to know its historical past from the “first” human being down to this very moment when the questions about it are being answered.
Every complete form of knowledge concerning any concrete thing or concrete human being is therefore perfect or absolute knowledge.
Let us now use another example to show that universal knowledge of oneself also includes the kind of knowledge normally called “philosophical” or “metaphysical.”
One only has to start answering almost any concrete question about oneself before the answers very quickly become “metaphysical.”
If I answer, “Because I like it and it gives me pleasure,” then the chain of questions comes to an abrupt end.
But by answering in this way, I am effectively admitting that I do not know why I wash—in other words, that I do not fully know who I am.
And in all honesty I cannot say that I particularly enjoy washing. When the water is cold, it can be positively unpleasant, yet I wash anyway.
So I am not doing it merely “instinctively.” I ought to be able to answer in words the question: “Why do you wash?”
Suppose I say: “For reasons of hygiene.”
With the very first answer, the difficulties begin.
“For reasons of hygiene” means: “because it is good for the health of my body.”
Let us assume that this is indeed true.
Why, then, am I so concerned about my body when this particular way of caring for it gives the body itself no immediate pleasure?
Because, we might answer, it is better to endure a short period of discomfort in exchange for a lasting benefit.
But now we have entered difficult territory.
Is something lasting always better than something brief?
Might it sometimes be right to sacrifice years of good health for a single minute of complete happiness?
Whatever answer we give, we are immediately drawn into difficult arguments that cannot be settled without concepts that are unmistakably “philosophical”—both “ethical” and “metaphysical.”
And, rather surprisingly, the argument can begin even earlier.
“Is it even worth caring about the body at all—and therefore worth washing it?”
There was a sect in India—and apparently it may still exist today—that regarded washing as a terrible, even “mortal,” sin.
Precisely because by washing oneself one cares for the body and therefore binds the soul to it, with the result that after death the soul falls into some miserable animal.
All of this may be nonsense. But these people existed, and they were not insane in the clinical sense. They gave meaningful answers to questions about their lives and conduct.
It is therefore possible, and even necessary, to argue with them.

But this argument becomes impossible unless we raise questions about the “soul” and the body, about the human being, immortality, God, and other issues of this kind—which are plainly metaphysical questions.
And it is easy to see that however we begin, once the questions concern ourselves we arrive very quickly at questions of this sort.
We can now sum up everything said so far.

On the one hand, our definition of philosophy as the ability to ask concrete questions about oneself does not break at all with the traditional idea of philosophy. The answers to these questions lead us inevitably—and very quickly—to problems that have always been called “philosophical” or “metaphysical.”

On the other hand, we have established that philosophical knowledge, as we understand it, is knowledge of oneself; and that this means concrete knowledge of a concrete human being, which in turn becomes complete knowledge of everything—perfect or “absolute” knowledge.
In saying this, we are not really departing from philosophical tradition, or at least from an important part of it.
Until quite recently, philosophical knowledge regarded itself as universal. Philosophers wanted to know everything.
And when some philosophers declared that “wisdom” was unattainable, they did so precisely because they did not identify themselves with the “sage” who possesses omniscience.
Yet although pre-Hegelian philosophy tried to know everything—or at least everything that could in principle be known—it was unable to show why this drive toward omniscience was necessary.
It is certainly better to know more rather than less. But the idea that one must know everything could easily appear to be an illusion.
Philosophers could therefore stop halfway and content themselves with partial knowledge.
From this point of view, philosophy could appear not very different from mathematics.
The mathematician also wants, in principle, to know everything that can be known mathematically. But a mathematician can restrict himself, say, to geometry.
He can exhaust that field completely without ever leaving it, and everything he knows within that field can still be perfectly or absolutely true.
It therefore seemed that omniscience in philosophy, just as in mathematics, might or might not be achieved. It seemed optional rather than necessary.
Everyone knew, of course, that unlike mathematics, which studies abstract and ideal objects, philosophers dealt with real things.
But the real sciences, such as physics and biology, could also do without omniscience. Perfect knowledge is not necessary for them.

One can, for example, study the physical properties of a living body without knowing its biological properties. Conversely, a biologist can study living organisms without knowing the structure of the atom.
This is possible because of the peculiar structure of real, material things.
As we have seen, complete knowledge of a concrete, real, material thing amounts to perfect knowledge or omniscience.
By contrast, knowledge of an abstract, ideal, non-material “thing” can be exhaustive while still remaining partial.
But it is possible to turn a concrete, real thing into an abstract “thing” that can become the object of partial yet apparently exhaustive knowledge.
Or, what comes to the same thing, complete knowledge of an “abstract thing” can function as partial but true knowledge of a concrete thing.

Complete knowledge of the geometrical properties of the ideal circle, for example, is certainly only partial knowledge of any real circle—say, the wheel of a car—but within its limits it is perfectly true.

Likewise, knowledge of the physical and chemical properties of “iron in general,” which is an ideal “thing” and as such never exists anywhere in reality, becomes partial knowledge of every real, concrete piece of iron and, more generally, of every concrete object containing iron.

Similarly, knowledge of ideal, abstract “things” such as “the plant in general” or “the fir tree in general” forms part of true knowledge of a particular fir tree—for example, the tree from which the boards in my desk were made.

So although complete knowledge of any concrete, real, material thing necessarily amounts to omniscience, it is still possible to have partial knowledge of that concrete thing that is nevertheless perfectly or absolutely true.
And if that is so, omniscience seems not strictly necessary, even if it remains desirable.
It is possible because, as we have already said, concrete, real, material things—like ideal, abstract “things”—possess qualities that, once given, are eternally unchanging.

The number of qualities belonging to a concrete thing may be so large that complete knowledge of them is practically impossible. But the qualities themselves are stable. So we can know some of them with complete truth and gradually expand our knowledge by moving from one to another.
This is precisely how science proceeds, and it might seem that philosophy can proceed in the same way.
To a certain extent, this is true when philosophy concerns itself with the material world.

The limit toward which philosophy aims is “wisdom,” or omniscience. And because partial scientific knowledge can be perfectly true, absolutely true philosophical omniscience must include scientific knowledge as one of its parts.
The road toward wisdom—philosophy in the proper sense of the word, which is itself still partial knowledge—therefore includes this absolutely true scientific knowledge.
But while the sciences restrict themselves in fact and in principle to partial knowledge, philosophy aims at perfect knowledge.
Because all sciences deal with abstract and ideal things, whereas philosophy seeks knowledge of concrete and real things.
And knowledge of concrete things is omniscience.
